topic: Matrix Multiplication as Composition of Linear Transformations
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Linear Algebra or Computer Graphics

sections.title: The Big Idea: Functions in Space
lecture_lines: Matrices aren't just boxes; they are transformations.
Think of a matrix as a verb moving space.
Meet Leo the Lion on our coordinate grid.
This rotation matrix tilts Leo ninety degrees.
The entire space transforms as a single unit.
animations: Fade in a coordinate grid in #444444.
Pulse the grid lines in #FFFFFF to suggest movement.
Fade in a Leo character at the origin; make him flash #FFFF00.
Rotate the grid and Leo 90 degrees CCW; show matrix [[0,-1],[1,0]] in #00FF00.
Scale Leo up (1.2x) and back to #FFFFFF to emphasize the completion of the unit transformation.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: The Basis Vectors
lecture_lines: We track transformation using unit basis vectors.
Watch i-hat and j-hat land at new coordinates.
These new locations form the matrix columns.
animations: Display unit vectors i-hat (1,0) in #FF0000 and j-hat (0,1) in #00FF00.
Smoothly animate i-hat moving to (0,1) and j-hat moving to (-1,0).
Fade in a 2x2 matrix with col1 as [0, 1] in #FF0000 and col2 as [-1, 0] in #00FF00.

sections.title: The Sequential Challenge: Two Steps, One Move
lecture_lines: Suppose we rotate then shear our character.
Applying two separate matrices takes two steps.
We want a single Master Matrix instead.
This shortcut is called matrix composition.
It skips the middle step entirely.
animations: Show Leo [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/leo.svg] at the origin on a standard grid.
Rotate Leo [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/leo.svg] 90 degrees CCW (Transformation A) in #00FF00.
Shear the rotated Leo [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/leo.svg] horizontally (Transformation B) in #00FFFF.
Clear the screen and display the text 'Master Matrix C' in #FFFFFF.
Apply Transformation C to the original Leo [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/leo.svg], moving him directly to the final sheared-rotated state.

sections.title: The Math: Why Right-to-Left?
lecture_lines: Matrix notation works from right to left.
The matrix closest to the vector acts first.
We combine these matrices into one single operation.
animations: Display 'B(A(x))' with A in #FFFF00, B in #00FFFF, and x in #FFFFFF.
Highlight A and x with a glowing #FFFF00 box to indicate precedence.
Morph the expression 'B * A' into a single matrix 'C' in #FFFFFF.

sections.title: Visual Derivation of the Product
lecture_lines: Track i-hat through the first rotation.
Next, apply the shear to its new position.
This final point becomes our first product column.
Follow j-hat to find the second column.
Now we have our composed transformation matrix.
animations: Show i-hat at (1,0) in #FF0000.
Rotate i-hat to (0,1) following a circular arc.
Shear i-hat from (0,1) to (1,1) along a horizontal line.
Circle the point (1,1) and place it as the first column of the result matrix.
Animate j-hat following its path to its final position and entering the second column.

sections.title: Summary and Non-Commutativity
lecture_lines: Matrix multiplication is just combining functions.
Does the order of transformations change the result?
Rotating then shearing is not shearing then rotating.
animations: Show two identical Leo characters [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/leo.svg] on split-screen grids.
Left: Animate Rotation then Shear; Right: Animate Shear then Rotation using the Leo assets [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/leo.svg].
Display a large red '≠' sign (#FF0000) between the two final states.
